title: Pruning Without Dying: Axons That Cut Themselves Back

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A target-supplied growth factor that a neuron needs to survive is a {{c1::trophic factor}}.
cards.back: NGF (nerve growth factor) is an example.
cards.quote: a growth factor, supplied by the target, that a neuron needs to survive.
cards.section: Lose support here, lose the branch here

cards.front: How does the location of NGF loss determine branch loss versus cell death in NGF-dependent sympathetic neurons?
cards.back: Local loss removes deprived branches if the cell body retains enough support. Loss from the whole neuron causes cell death during its NGF-dependent window.
cards.quote: take the trophic signal away from its axons, or some of them, while the cell body still has enough support, and the deprived axons degenerate
cards.section: Lose support here, lose the branch here

cards.front: In a compartmented culture of NGF-dependent sympathetic neurons, NGF is absent around cell bodies and proximal neurites but remains at distal neurite ends. Must the neurons die, and why?
cards.back: No; they can survive. Support received at distal neurite ends can suffice, so every part of a neurite need not be directly bathed in NGF.
cards.quote: the cell bodies and the near ends of the neurites could do without it, as long as the far ends reached NGF.
cards.section: Lose support here, lose the branch here

cards.front: Which neurons and pruning trigger fall within the rule that the location of lost NGF support determines what is lost?
cards.back: NGF-dependent sympathetic and sensory neurons during their dependence window; local degeneration after trophic loss, including competition. It excludes pruning selected by a developmental program.
cards.quote: NGF-dependent sympathetic neurons, and NGF-dependent sensory neurons, during their window of dependence.
cards.section: Lose support here, lose the branch here

cards.front: How do progressive and regressive events contribute differently to nervous-system development?
cards.back: Progressive events build the draft: neuron birth, migration, layers and axon targeting. Regressive events sculpt it through neuron death, synapse removal and branch pruning.
cards.quote: Regressive events then sculpt the circuits: whole neurons die, synapses are removed, and axons and dendrites are pruned.
cards.section: Building, then sculpting

cards.front: Removal of an axon branch or dendrite from a neuron that survives is called {{c1::pruning}}.
cards.back: Whole-neuron death is a separate regressive event.
cards.quote: removal of an axon branch or a dendrite from a neuron that survives.
cards.section: Building, then sculpting

cards.front: How does branch removal by retraction differ from removal by local degeneration?
cards.back: Retraction pulls a branch toward the cell body, returning much of its material. Local degeneration breaks it into pieces in place for other cells to engulf.
cards.why: Some retracting branches also shed small pieces that glia engulf; debris alone does not establish local degeneration.
cards.quote: In local degeneration, the branch breaks into pieces in place, and other cells engulf the pieces.
cards.section: Building, then sculpting

cards.front: Branch removal specified by a genetic program is {{c1::stereotyped pruning}}.
cards.back: The same branch is selected in every animal.
cards.quote: In stereotyped pruning the branch to be removed is set by a genetic program, so the same branch goes in every animal.
cards.section: Building, then sculpting

cards.front: In a hypothetical developing circuit, changing which axon obtains limited target-derived support changes which branch survives. What pruning trigger does this support?
cards.back: Competitive pruning: branch survival follows success in obtaining support rather than a fixed branch identity specified by a program.
cards.quote: In competitive pruning the outcome depends on competition between axons, for example for trophic support, or through differences in activity.
cards.section: Building, then sculpting

cards.front: How do initiator and executioner caspases divide the work during apoptosis?
cards.back: Initiator caspases start the cascade by activating executioner caspases; executioners carry out proteolytic dismantling.
cards.quote: Initiator caspases, such as caspase-9, start a cascade that switches on executioner caspases
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: Design a culture experiment in NGF-dependent mouse sympathetic neurons to distinguish local branch pruning from whole-neuron death caused by NGF loss. Which outcomes must be scored separately?
cards.back: Use fluid-isolated axon and cell-body compartments. Compare axon-only withdrawal, withdrawal from both compartments and maintained support. Score axon integrity and cell-body survival separately. The rules predict local loss with soma survival versus whole-cell death.
cards.quote: Local deprivation: remove NGF from the axon compartment only. Global deprivation: remove NGF from both compartments.
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: NGF is withdrawn either from axons alone or from the entire culture of caspase-6-null mouse sympathetic neurons. How do axon outcomes differ, and why?
cards.back: Axons are protected after local withdrawal but degenerate with dying neurons after global withdrawal. Local pruning requires caspase-6; axon loss accompanying whole-cell apoptosis does not.
cards.quote: After global deprivation, deleting caspase-6 no longer saved the axons: they degenerated as the neurons died, since axon breakdown during whole-cell death rides on apoptosis.
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: Which caspases were required for local pruning after axon-only NGF withdrawal in mouse sympathetic neurons?
cards.back: Caspase-9, caspase-3 and caspase-6.
cards.quote: Local pruning needed caspase-9, caspase-3 and caspase-6.
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: Apaf-1-null mouse sympathetic neurons undergo either axon-only or whole-culture NGF withdrawal. What happens to locally deprived axons and to globally deprived cell bodies, and why?
cards.back: Locally deprived axons still degenerate while cell bodies survive. Globally deprived neurons resist death. Local pruning bypasses Apaf-1, whereas whole-neuron apoptosis requires it.
cards.quote: In this study, local pruning did not need Apaf-1, and death of the whole neuron did.
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: Why does combining the Apaf-1-null and caspase-6-null results provide stronger evidence for distinct local-pruning and whole-cell-death routes than the caspase-6 result alone?
cards.back: Caspase-6 loss protects only against local pruning; Apaf-1 loss protects against whole-cell death while allowing local pruning. These reciprocal requirements support differently wired routes sharing caspases, rather than one route merely receiving different signal strengths.
cards.quote: Each route needs something the other does not, which points to two differently wired routes that share enzymes
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: In a hypothetical NGF-withdrawal experiment, 80% of wild-type axon fields and 16% of mutant fields show degeneration at 48 hours. The mutant degeneration fraction is what percentage of the wild-type fraction?
cards.back: (16% / 80%) × 100% = 20%. The mutant fraction is one fifth of the wild-type fraction.
cards.quote: Without it, locally deprived axons were spared.
cards.section: One neuron, two ways to lose an axon

cards.front: How do XIAP and the proteasome help a mouse sympathetic neuron survive local axon pruning?
cards.back: They keep caspases off in the cell body. XIAP binds and blocks active caspase-9 and caspase-3, protecting the part that must survive.
cards.quote: XIAP, a protein that binds and blocks active caspase-9 and caspase-3, and the proteasome kept caspases switched off in the cell bodies.
cards.section: Guarding the part that must live

cards.front: The cell machinery that destroys proteins tagged with ubiquitin is the {{c1::proteasome}}.
cards.quote: The proteasome is the cell's machine for destroying proteins tagged with ubiquitin
cards.section: Guarding the part that must live

cards.front: Axonal NGF is withdrawn from XIAP-null mouse sympathetic neurons while cell-body NGF remains. What change in cell-body caspase activity is expected, and why?
cards.back: Active caspase-3 accumulates in cell bodies because the XIAP inhibitor is absent. This result alone does not establish that the neurons die.
cards.quote: After local deprivation, neurons lacking XIAP built up active caspase-3 in their cell bodies.
cards.section: Guarding the part that must live

cards.front: In metamorphosing fly sensory neurons, a caspase reporter lights up only in disappearing dendrites, and suppressing caspases preserves those dendrites. What do the two observations show?
cards.back: Caspase activity is spatially restricted to the pruned dendrites and is required for their removal. Reporter localization alone would show location, not necessity.
cards.quote: It appeared only in the dendrites being removed. Suppressing caspases kept the dendrites
cards.section: Guarding the part that must live

cards.front: In the proposed fly sensory-dendrite pruning model, how does ubiquitin tagging release Dronc from inhibition?
cards.back: UbcD1 helps send the inhibitor DIAP1 to the proteasome, releasing Dronc. How this process remains confined to dendrites is not fully worked out.
cards.quote: The ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme UbcD1 helps send DIAP1, an inhibitor that holds the fly caspase Dronc in check, to the proteasome.
cards.section: Guarding the part that must live

cards.front: A hypothetical manipulation prevents DIAP1 removal only in selected fly sensory dendrites. Under the proposed model, what happens there, and how does this compare with XIAP protection of mouse sympathetic cell bodies?
cards.back: Those dendrites should retain Dronc inhibition and resist pruning. The shared rule is that retained caspase inhibitors protect a compartment. Fly DIAP1 removal is a proposed mechanism with unresolved localization; mouse XIAP protection of cell bodies was demonstrated.
cards.quote: Where that removal happens, and how caspase activity stays in the dendrites and out of the cell body, is not fully worked out.
cards.section: Guarding the part that must live

cards.front: Why can loss of some branches leave an NGF-dependent sympathetic neuron alive rather than trigger whole-cell death?
cards.back: Remaining branches can provide enough target-derived support to the cell body. Survival depends on the overall trophic signal reaching it, not a fixed count of lost branches.
cards.quote: the whole neuron dies when too little of that signal reaches the cell body overall, not after some fixed number of branches lose it.
cards.section: Winners and losers: who loses a contest

cards.front: Which receptor transduces NGF signalling in the sympathetic-axon competition model, and what receptor class does it belong to?
cards.back: TrkA, a receptor tyrosine kinase.
cards.quote: TrkA is the NGF receptor tyrosine kinase.
cards.section: Winners and losers: who loses a contest

cards.front: BDNF reaches competing sympathetic axons with unequal TrkA signalling. Which axons are vulnerable, which receptor mediates degeneration, and why are the others protected?
cards.back: Axons with weak TrkA signalling are vulnerable to BDNF-driven degeneration through p75. Strong TrkA signalling protects the competing axons from that signal.
cards.quote: On axons with weak TrkA signalling, BDNF acting through p75 caused degeneration, while axons with strong TrkA signalling were protected.
cards.section: Winners and losers: who loses a contest

cards.front: In the sympathetic-axon competition model, how does a winning axon actively contribute to removing a loser?
cards.back: Winning neurons make BDNF; in one model, winning axons release it in an activity-dependent way. BDNF acts through p75 on weakly TrkA-signalling losers.
cards.quote: In one model, winning axons release BDNF in an activity-dependent way.
cards.section: Winners and losers: who loses a contest

cards.front: What are the three phases of NGF-deprived sympathetic axon degeneration, in order?
cards.back: Latent: axon looks nearly normal. Transition: spheroid swellings appear late in latency. Catastrophic: axon fragments.
cards.quote: Transition. Late in latency, swellings called axonal spheroids appear. Catastrophic phase. The axon fragments.
cards.section: When a deprived axon commits

cards.front: In the lesson’s study of NGF-deprived sympathetic axons, which calcium and membrane-surface changes make spheroids distinct sites?
cards.back: Calcium rises before catastrophe and gathers in spheroids. Spheroids alone expose phosphatidylserine, a lipid recognized by phagocytes.
cards.quote: Spheroids, but not the rest of the axon, exposed phosphatidylserine, a membrane lipid that phagocytes recognize.
cards.section: When a deprived axon commits

cards.front: During NGF-deprived axon degeneration, spheroids admit 3- and 10-kilodalton dextran tracers but exclude 70-kilodalton tracers. What does entry reveal about their membranes?
cards.back: The membrane barrier has been compromised: these tracers cannot cross an intact membrane. Permeability is selective under these conditions; exclusion of the larger tracer argues against unrestricted entry.
cards.quote: Then they ruptured, letting in dextran tracers, sugar chains that cannot cross an intact membrane, of 3 and 10 kilodaltons but not of 70
cards.section: When a deprived axon commits

cards.front: Conditioned medium from NGF-deprived axons accelerates fragmentation of fresh NGF-deprived axons. What can be concluded about communication between the axons?
cards.back: Deprived axons release something into the medium that accelerates catastrophe in other deprived axons. This experiment does not identify the released substance.
cards.quote: conditioned medium, sped fresh deprived axons into catastrophe, so deprived axons release something that does this.
cards.section: When a deprived axon commits

cards.front: In the lesson’s sympathetic-axon study, how do p75 and DR6 divide the work in spheroid formation and conditioned-medium-accelerated catastrophe after NGF deprivation?
cards.back: p75 is needed for spheroid formation; DR6 is not. DR6 is needed for the accelerated catastrophe; p75 is not.
cards.quote: p75 was needed for spheroids to form, and DR6 was not.
cards.section: When a deprived axon commits

cards.front: Forcing Rho activity in p75-null, NGF-deprived axons restores spheroids and degeneration. How does this connect p75 to Rho, and does it prove that spheroids gate commitment?
cards.back: The rescue supports Rho acting downstream of p75 and fits the model that spheroids gate commitment. It does not prove that gate: restoring spheroids and degeneration together does not isolate spheroids as the cause.
cards.quote: forcing Rho on in p75-null axons restored both spheroids and degeneration. That fits a gate but does not prove one
cards.section: When a deprived axon commits

cards.front: How are the timing and cellular selectivity of fly mushroom body gamma-neuron remodeling coordinated at metamorphosis?
cards.back: Rising 20-hydroxyecdysone supplies timing. EcR-B1 expression in gamma neurons helps select responders; EcR-B1 and its partner USP are required within the remodeling neuron.
cards.quote: The hormone gives the timing; the receptor helps decide which neurons respond.
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: A nuclear receptor is a ligand-activated {{c1::transcription factor}}.
cards.quote: The ecdysone receptor is a nuclear receptor, a ligand-activated transcription factor
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: During fly mushroom body gamma-neuron remodeling, larval branches bleb and become disconnected fragments while the main axon shaft stays continuous. Which physical pruning process fits this record, and why?
cards.back: Local degeneration: branches fragment in place. Retraction would preserve branch continuity as the branch pulled back toward the cell.
cards.quote: Separated pieces are what local degeneration predicts, since a retracting branch would stay connected to the cell.
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: Why does fragmentation alone fail to establish that fly mushroom body gamma-axon pruning uses the same death machinery as local NGF-deprived mouse axons?
cards.back: Mouse local pruning needs caspases. Blocking main apoptosis activators or expressing p35 did not stop fly gamma-axon pruning, which therefore does not appear to require usual apoptosis machinery.
cards.quote: blocking the fly's main apoptosis activators or expressing p35 did not stop this axon pruning
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: In a hypothetical fly mosaic, only gamma neurons with disrupted ubiquitin tagging retain normal larval branches during metamorphic pruning; neighboring neurons prune. What requirement does this pattern support?
cards.back: Ubiquitin tagging is required within the pruning neuron for branch removal. Initial branch formation occurred, and normal neighbors do not restore pruning in the altered cells.
cards.quote: blocking ubiquitin tagging, or the proteasome, kept the larval branches in place. The requirement was inside the pruning neuron.
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: What does persistence of the hippocampal infrapyramidal tract in neuropilin-2-null or Plexin-A3-null mice show about the Sema3F pathway?
cards.back: The receptor pathway is required for later tract pruning: the tract forms but stays long. Later work also showed Sema3F itself is required.
cards.quote: in mice lacking neuropilin-2 or Plexin-A3, parts of the receptor for the repulsive cue Sema3F, the tract stayed long
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: Can the rule linking lost trophic support to local branch loss explain both fly gamma-neuron remodeling and mouse hippocampal infrapyramidal-tract pruning? Identify the trigger and physical process in each.
cards.back: No. The rule concerns degeneration after local trophic loss. Fly gamma axons undergo hormone-driven, stereotyped local degeneration; the mouse tract undergoes Sema3F-dependent retraction. Developmental programs can select branches without lost trophic support.
cards.quote: a hormone or a repulsive cue triggers the pruning, and no loss of trophic support is needed to explain it.
cards.section: When a program, not support, picks the branch

cards.front: After global NGF withdrawal, Apaf-1-null sympathetic cell bodies resist death. A report calls their axon preservation a model prediction. Why must that claim remain distinct from the observed cell-body result?
cards.back: The whole-cell route requires Apaf-1, so the model predicts axon preservation when apoptosis is blocked. Cell-body survival alone is not an axon measurement; local pruning can also destroy axons while cell bodies live.
cards.quote: Apaf-1-null neurons resist that death, and Cusack and colleagues' model predicts their axons are spared too.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In the mouse sympathetic-neuron experiments, which Bcl-2 family protein is required for both local NGF-deprivation-induced axon degeneration and whole-neuron apoptosis?
cards.back: Bax. Its action in the Apaf-1-independent local route remains unsettled.
cards.quote: So both routes need Bax as well as caspase-9 and caspase-3.
cards.section: Bax in both routes

cards.front: A timing experiment compares mutant sympathetic axons after local NGF withdrawal with wild-type axons after global withdrawal. Can a different latency be attributed to the mutation? How should the comparison be repaired?
cards.back: No: deprivation mode is confounded with genotype. Compare mutant and wild type under the same withdrawal condition, with supported controls. The relevant rule is that local and global deprivation produce different latent phases.
cards.quote: local and global NGF deprivation give different latent phases
cards.section: Latent phases differ with the kind of deprivation

cards.front: Why should protection by WldS after axon injury not be taken as evidence that WldS blocks developmental axon pruning?
cards.back: Protection depends on the degeneration context: WldS strongly protects injured axons but did not block the developmental pruning tested. Injury protection cannot establish protection in developmental pruning.
cards.quote: WldS did not block the developmental axon pruning Hoopfer and colleagues tested
cards.section: Wallerian degeneration, WldS, SARM1 and DR6 after injury

cards.front: An initial injury study reports that DR6 promotes axon degeneration; a later study using two DR6 knockout lines finds no such effect. Does the combined evidence establish a universal requirement for DR6 after injury?
cards.back: No. The reported results conflict, so this evidence does not settle the role of DR6 after injury. The initial positive result cannot establish a universal requirement.
cards.quote: a 2026 study with two DR6 knockout lines found no such effect
cards.section: Wallerian degeneration, WldS, SARM1 and DR6 after injury
